title: New Minister, Same Challenges: Development Priorities Under Scrutiny
label: 15 September 2026 · Minister Kirsty McNeill's first appearance
summary: In her first appearance before the International Development Committee, Minister Kirsty McNeill set out continuity with the previous approach—including the Africa strategy and a bias towards multilateral spending—alongside new emphases on a 'values-led' approach, five 'securities' (health, climate, food, human, economic) and a focus on women, girls and young people. She defended the decision to cut bilateral aid while protecting multilateral spending, argued that ODA is 'the right instrument for some things, not everything', and faced sustained questioning on the 0.7% target, cuts to the World Food Programme, Israel/Palestine policy, Ukraine, Sudan, and FCDO restructuring. Nick Dyer provided operational detail on restructures, ICAI, communities of expertise, and the Chelsea fund.

chapters.title: Introductions and Continuity
chapters.takeaway: The new Minister promised continuity on Africa, the four shifts and allocations, but flagged a new focus on values, five 'securities' and children.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, both. Minister, can you introduce yourself and Nick, and outline your vision and priorities for international development?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I am Kirsty McNeill, MP for Midlothian and Minister of State for Development and Africa. This is my first time here but it won't be my last. Helping to drive performance through transparency and accountability to you will be incredibly important to me.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: I am Nick Dyer, one of the two permanent secretaries at the FCDO. I'll remain interim until the new permanent secretary formally starts on 19 October.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: There will be continuity on the Africa approach and on the four shifts: from donor to investor, service delivery to systems support, grants to expertise, and international interventions to local leadership.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Allocations are not up for being reopened. Inside them is a focus on multilaterals and what we can achieve working with others.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Three new flavours: first, being unapologetic about a values-led approach—saving and changing lives overseas in our partner countries is the core purpose.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Second, the five securities: health, climate, food, human and economic security. The security frame talks about mutual interests of north and south and brings the full capability of the FCDO to bear.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Third, renewed focus on who development is for: women and girls—beyond VAWG—and children and young people. I want that in every submission.

chapters.title: The Africa Approach
chapters.takeaway: The Africa strategy is more honest and transactional, but still human-rights based and country-specific, not one-size-fits-all.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I have never been entirely convinced by the Africa approach. It seemed to treat African nations as a homogenous lump. What does it mean to you?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Lord Collins did intensive consultations. Across government, private sector and civil society the message was: 'Just be brisk and businesslike. We don't mind transactional, we want deals in our mutual interest.'

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Other partners were more straightforward about what they wanted. Colleagues said, 'We don't mind if Britain is like that. Just be straightforward.'

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: The Africa approach is more honest about the fact that we have foreign policy objectives across the continent as well as development ones.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: But I come from a human rights-based approach. Brisk with Governments, yes, because they are the duty bearers—but equitable partnership means not taking a vow of silence when we think they are wrong.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: To what extent have we seen success in that transactional, commercial approach?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: It's going relatively well. Nigeria and Ghana on growth is different from elsewhere where it's more security and critical minerals. In my bilateral conversations, African Ministers would say each relationship is specific to that country.

chapters.title: Multilaterals vs Bilateral
chapters.takeaway: The Minister has a strong bias towards scaled impact through multilaterals, but wants reform and better storytelling about results.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: How do you tie that with backing multilaterals more than bilateral support?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Bilateral is good for attributed impact; multilaterals are good for scaled impact. Personally I have a strong bias towards scaled impact and am willing to trade off quite a lot of national attribution to get results for communities.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: Our report on the future of aid critiqued how transparent the attributed impact is to the public. Do you think our bilateral institutions are having the attributed impact you describe?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: The bias towards multilateralism is not uncritical. Three challenges: effectiveness—not uniformly delivered; representation—southern voice not where it should be; and transparency. The Foreign Secretary becoming World Bank governor was to drive that reform.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: People accept our Gavi contribution because we can say it will immunise 109 million children. We don't do that enough with the World Bank. We talk about £1.98 billion—but we should talk about the 300 million people getting energy access and 80 million children educated. We talk too much about the money we put in.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: Do we do that well enough for bilateral programming? Transparency around impact is often lacking.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We track programmes and can tell the stories. Ministers challenge us to lead with impact stories, not money commitments. We have to get much better at it.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Honestly, we just haven't had the level of ministerial confidence in telling the story about why aid works. I'm happy to be out there in the argument—there will be scepticism, but we should take it head on.

chapters.title: Cabinet Seat and Cross-Government Working
chapters.takeaway: The Minister is relaxed about not being in Cabinet, focusing instead on a reconstituted ODA board to drive policy coherence across Government.

turns.speaker: Janet Daby
turns.text: Baroness Chapman had a Cabinet seat. How can you carry out your role effectively without attending Cabinet?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I'm profoundly relaxed about that—I'm not motivated by the status. If a Cabinet seat is a mechanism for cross-Government conversations, as long as that can be secured another way, I'm relaxed.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: We're looking at reconstituting the cross-Government ODA board so it still does the accounting function but operates much more as a policy-coherence-for-development board. Hold me to account on whether we deliver that.

turns.speaker: Janet Daby
turns.text: In Cabinet you can speak directly to Secretaries of State and things move faster. How do you navigate those conversations?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: The Foreign Secretary sees development and climate as right at the heart of British foreign policy, not an adjunct. He'll be making the case in every Cabinet meeting and giving me licence to roam Whitehall.

chapters.title: Europe, US and Trade
chapters.takeaway: The UK is re-engaging with EU development partners for the first time since Brexit, while working around the US aid cuts through agile alliances.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: How are discussions with European allies progressing on development?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Breaking news: I've been invited to the EU Development Ministers' meeting—the first time a British Development Minister has been invited since Brexit. I'll go in early October.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: Last month I had the first development and humanitarian dialogue with the European Commission since Brexit. The first in 10 years. The relationship has been reset at official and ministerial levels.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: What technical work is being done to align with EU partners?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We've identified two or three themes where working teams are coming together. The European Commission is going into its next financial perspectives next year, so there'll be a reset in how it interprets development policy.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I'd welcome your scrutiny on how we use our embassies in European capitals to talk about development. One benefit of having the Development Minister in the FCDO is the ability to pull on the whole network.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: What conversations are you having with the US about their position on international development? USAID cuts were massive.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We have dialogues on the Hill and through the G20 with the US Treasury. On development it's harder—many established entry points have disappeared. The key US official responsible for development was just moved. We look for entry points, and the G7 Development Ministers' meeting will include the current US counterpart.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: State governors are interested in global health. Is that a partnership you might have?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I can't say whether we are, but agile alliances mean we'd like to speak to all sorts of levels of government. Nick, do you have anything to add?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: At state level we've engaged on climate in the past. Whether on health, I'd have to check with the Department of Health.

chapters.title: Public Communication and Civil Society
chapters.takeaway: The real public scepticism is about whether aid works, not about moral purpose—so the Minister wants to make the effectiveness case and engage civil society on substance, not set-piece meetings.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: You've talked about the five securities, but WASH runs through every one. Our report raised concerns about Government engagement with the public on aid. What will your approach be?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: You're right to pick up on the relationship between food, water and energy security. I folded water and energy alongside food conceptually. I hope you forgive me for not calling them out directly.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: On public communication: I've never met someone who says they don't care at all about people dying overseas. The scepticism is: 'Does this work? If it works and we can afford it, we should do more.' It's about effectiveness, not moral purpose.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: You're right about water—25% of people don't have safely managed water. We shifted from direct service delivery to improving systems and leveraging finance. The Water Forward initiative aims for another 1 billion people to gain access, with the World Bank contributing 400 million.

turns.speaker: Dr Rushworth
turns.text: Bilateral aid has taken the big hit from protecting multilateral spend. What's the likely impact on bilateral relationships?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Our proportion to Africa will be pretty steady because of imputed multilateral spend. But African capitals don't want the conversation to be about aid. I'm clear to African Ministers that I'm not the aid Minister.

turns.speaker: Dr Rushworth
turns.text: Often a pound can be spent more effectively at grassroots, yet FCDO tendering excludes smaller charities. What are you doing?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We recognise that major reporting requirements make small organisations fall over. We're looking at making programme requirements more proportionate and doing due diligence once. For too long we've squeezed out small organisations just because of the way we do business.

turns.speaker: Dr Rushworth
turns.text: How do you plan to engage with UK INGOs as intermediaries?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We have a 10-year programme with Comic Relief looking at building local organisations. We have examples of engaging directly with local organisations rather than through third parties. This is a big question if you want to drive funding through local organisations—USAID tried and didn't fully succeed.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: My approach to civil society is about real things—substantive conversations about where we agree, disagree, and what we can do together. I'm not in the business of set-piece, choreographed, lowest-common-denominator meetings.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I hope you'd go further and talk to the actual individuals living the issue—like a fisherwoman who knows the solution. Do you have appetite to go more granular?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Forgive me—I was talking about UK civil society. I've asked that time with children and young people and women be programmed into each visit. In Ethiopia I visited a one-stop shop for survivors of sexual violence and met women on social protection who got business mentoring. Those experiences will stay with me.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: Thirty years ago at ODA I co-designed projects with communities. As we scaled up to 0.7% we became a wholesaler, not a retailer. We don't have the resources to run projects directly. Micro-projects would need a lot of people on the ground—very expensive.

chapters.title: Restructuring, ICAI and Communities of Expertise
chapters.takeaway: The FCDO restructure is proceeding in phases; the Minister is confident ICAI can still scrutinise despite cuts, and communities of expertise are still being worked through.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What steps have you taken to ensure you have the skills in the team to deliver your vision?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Colleagues have two questions: capability—I'm as satisfied as one can reasonably be that we've retained what we need; and culture—whether development is still valued. The new permanent secretary comes from a DFID background, and the Foreign Secretary has been clear about the priority he puts on development.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How are you giving them stability after six years of turbulence?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I've been explicit about telegraphing back what we're doing in my trips. Our colleagues toil in unbelievably difficult circumstances. I was humbled by the psychological resilience and physical courage required to operate in Mogadishu. Morale is partly my job.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The London restructure is managed centrally but posts manage their own. How is the pipeline of skills being linked?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: The UK restructuring has been in advance of overseas. We launched the new structure last Monday. The overseas network is a second phase—we haven't finalised decisions. We need to ask whether we have the capability to deliver the shifts and whether it makes sense for a rotational workforce. Over 10 years, UK-based staff grew 40%, overseas didn't grow at all. That will balance better.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What reassurance for East Kilbride staff?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I'm going to be there at least once a quarter, hopefully more—I live in Scotland. I wanted to get there quickly to reassure them face to face that we're completely committed to them.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: ICAI got a 40% cut while King Charles Street got 25%. Can it still fulfil its legally mandated role?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I believe it can. I met the chief commissioner last week. I differentiate between its legally mandated role and the wider transparency agenda. It won't be the only driver of our transparency and performance—I'm committed to scrutiny from as many sources as possible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Where are communities of expertise at? Each time we ask, the title changes.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: This is about the shift from service delivery to system support—making world-class expertise available to countries on demand. It will take two to three years to build. We have nine communities of expertise, and some have been in existence for some time.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is it like a living library, research centre and signposting?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: There's not one standard model. We're struggling with whether to bring one brand and consistent approach to all of this. I wouldn't sit here saying it's all perfect. We know what we're doing, but bringing it into effect is tricky.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about the money—does the centre decide where it goes, or do posts?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: It's a mixed model. Some posts have their own resources; others rely on the centre. In one early model we gave money to countries, but a lot didn't want the transaction costs—they'd rather it was centralised and drawn down quickly.

chapters.title: Ukraine, Chelsea Fund and Israel/Palestine
chapters.takeaway: The Minister defended the Ukraine allocation, said the Chelsea fund proceeds must be released urgently, and argued the Israel policy shift keeps the two-state solution alive.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: How do you see the UK's ODA commitment to Ukraine evolving?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I'm proud of it. It's a big allocation from a shrinking pot, so I dug into it with colleagues in Kyiv. The three-year allocation is about £240 million a year and will stay at that sort of level.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: The really big sums are the $5 billion of guarantees for fiscal support. If you can't fund the fiscal side of the Government, that's war-losing. On the humanitarian side, the need is just as high as it has been. The war is still going on, so I expect that to continue.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: What's the current position on releasing the Chelsea fund proceeds?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: We are 100% clear that the proceeds urgently need to be released. Mr Abramovich committed over four years ago. We created the OFSI licence in December. There cannot be further delays—we're urgently exploring further action, including preparing for a possible legal case.

turns.speaker: David Taylor
turns.text: Many groups donate convoys of supplies to Ukraine. Joint work between FCDO and MOD would help with paperwork and delays. Could we pick that up again?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We'll take that away and come back to you.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: The Foreign Office shut the unit tracking potential law breaches by Israel—the IHL cell—and funding to the Centre for Information Resilience. How will you effect change if you're blind to what's going on?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: The IHL cell hasn't disappeared; the 21 staff are now working in the export control unit. The work continues. On the Centre for Information Resilience, we still have access to its reports, and we rely on open-source information, NGO reports and feedback on the ground.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do we have access to the historical data already collated?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We certainly have access to the data already collated. I'll check on the other data and come back to you.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: The Foreign Secretary has been clear about the significance of the policy change on settlements and the legality of the occupation. What remains unchanged is our humanitarian commitment to the Palestinian people. This change is to keep the prospect of a two-state solution alive.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: It's disappointing to hear it called a policy change. The ICJ ruling was two years ago. Our international credibility has been dented because we didn't follow the clear rules of law.

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I wouldn't characterise it as a surprise to the Department. It's a significant shift in UK policy. You'll hear a lot more from the Foreign Secretary on this.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: 1.4 million people in Gaza face acute food insecurity, yet the UK cut funding to the World Food Programme by 78% since 2024. Why does that make sense?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: The interim executive director of WFP impressed on me that we face choices that are the stuff of nightmares—responding to emergencies versus investing in long-term resilience. I'd welcome your challenge on whether we're getting the balance right.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: The issue in Gaza is not money; it is access. Averting famine cannot be a measure of success. We know why dual-use goods aren't getting in—it's the actions of the Israeli Government. We need more crossing points and Israel to live up to its commitments.

chapters.title: Sudan, Ebola and Rapid Fire
chapters.takeaway: The Minister promised more on Sudan, defended the Ebola response, and said women and girls remain central while children may get an explicit priority.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: Will there be a shift in how the Government approaches Sudan?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Expect to hear more from us on Sudan in coming weeks and months. Both I and the Foreign Secretary have sought briefings from day one. We're going to strain every diplomatic sinew to get an enduring settlement.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: How is the UK supporting efforts to contain Ebola?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I announced extra funding two weeks ago. Africa CDC and the African Union said British money is fast and wise. We're disbursing fast while other donors haven't moved as quickly.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: How is the vaccination programme developing?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: The first trial, including Oxford, has started. This is now the second largest Ebola outbreak ever. We've been playing catch-up. This is a marathon, not a sprint—it will go on for two years.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: What priority are you placing on strengthening food systems and addressing malnutrition?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: A huge priority. Food security is the thing that keeps me awake most at night. Organisationally, food currently sits in humanitarian, but it needs to sit alongside climate, health, economic and human security. It's so cross-cutting.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: When will the National Action Plan on women, peace and security be published, and the monitoring framework?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I can't give a date, but the fact that it's a refresh is a sign of how highly we prize it. We want to crack on and scale it rather than restarting. I'll get back to you.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: Will the FCDO collate data on how projects engage women and girls, people with disabilities, LGBT communities and other minorities?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Yes, human rights and equalities will be ongoing. Minister Elmore leads on that. I give a very public undertaking: women and girls is central to everything. VAWG is the floor, not the ceiling. Hold me to account.

turns.speaker: Dr Rushworth
turns.text: UNICEF found bilateral aid for child-focused programmes cut by 57% from 2019 to 2023. Will you make children an explicit priority of Government?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: I've received persuasive representations on mechanisms—like a special envoy for children. I won't pre-empt where we land, but I want to underscore my ambition. I'm taking advice on how to put children and young people at the heart. Maybe next time I can commit on the mechanism.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: I don't actually recognise that number.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On UN80, the Secretary-General proposed merging UN Women and UNFPA. What's your view?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Minister Elmore holds the decision. We don't want to see the mandate of either organisation reopened—we stand four-square behind them. But we also think it's a progressive imperative to make the UN slimmer. We're balancing those. Minister Elmore will come back to you.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: Have the FCDO's strategic priorities on climate and nature changed under new leadership?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: Substantively, no, but the level of primacy this agenda has in all our diplomacy has rocketed up.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: How will you deliver the UK's international climate finance commitments effectively?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: It will be a huge feature of upcoming multilateral settings. The Foreign Secretary and I have a discussion tabled on financing tomorrow. He's happy to spend significant international political capital on it.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We'll be tracking that £6 billion commitment over the next three years.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: What reforms of the multilaterals are you looking at to increase climate finance flows?

turns.speaker: Kirsty McNeill
turns.text: We'll want to come back to you on that—it's going to be a huge part of our G20 agenda. Perhaps a chunky session on it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We'll be publishing our report on international climate finance on Thursday. We hope it's a practical tool. Thank you both for being so generous with your time. We hope this is a regular occurrence.
